title: What is the 'Eng' in 'England'? | COUNTRY NAME ORIGINS

entries.note: First published in 1507 by [[see:Martin Waldseemüller]] and [[see:Matthias Ringmann]], after [[from:Amerigo Vespucci]]. It was made feminine like many country names and first applied to South America.
Explorer whose disputed voyages, known mainly from letters like the [[see:Soderini letter]], got [[see:America]] named after him; his stilt-house comparison also inspired [[see:Venezuela]].
German cartographer whose 1507 wall map and globe first named [[see:America]]; Rob says his surname means something like forest lake miller.
Circle of humanist scholars in Saint-Dié, founded around 1500 under the Duke of Lorraine, which turned from a new edition of Ptolemy to the work that named [[see:America]].
Disputed 1506 letter crediting [[see:Amerigo Vespucci]] with discovering a new continent; its French translation led to the naming of [[see:America]].
The book that contained [[see:Martin Waldseemüller]]'s wall map and globe, which explicitly named the new continent [[see:America]].
Huge map that went with the [[see:Cosmographiae Introductio]] and also labelled the new continent [[see:America]].
Reached the Caribbean in 1492, before Vespucci's voyages. His surname means dove, from Latin [[from:columba]], and he [[gave:Colombia]] and [[gave:Columbia]] their names.
A feminine Latin word for land, given as one reason why countries such as [[see:America]] are often feminine.
From Englaland, land of the [[from:Angles]]. Almost every language names it after them, except Irish, which calls it [[see:Sasana]].
Germanic tribe who settled Britain more fully than the [[see:Saxons]], bringing their royals and ruling powerful kingdoms, so [[gave:England]] is named after them.
Germanic tribe that came to Britain but kept a homeland in [[see:Saxony]]; the Irish [[see:Sasana]] names England after them.
One of three Germanic tribes, with the [[see:Angles]] and [[see:Saxons]], said to have taken over parts of Britain after the Romans left.
Region in Germany named after the [[see:Saxons]], used to explain why England was named after the Angles instead.
The Irish name for [[see:England]], meaning land of the [[see:Saxons]]; it is the exception to naming England after the Angles.
Shortened to [[see:America]] because the founding fathers committed to that name, an example of branding in country names.
The states of the US are really provinces; that is what a state means now, but it doesn't meet the earlier definitions.
Named from the same Germanic word as [[same-root:Welsh]]; its start is the same sound as the end of [[same-root:Cornwall]].
From Germanic [[from:walh]], used for speakers of a foreign tongue. It only later came to mean slave in English, because Celts were commonly enslaved.
Word the continental Germanic tribes used for Romance-speaking peoples, later applied to Celtic speakers in Britain; it [[gave:walnut]], [[gave:Walloons]] and [[gave:Welsh]].
Means nut of the Romance-speaking people, from [[from:walh]].
The French speakers of Belgium, whose name also comes from [[from:walh]].
From [[from:Slav]], because Slavs were commonly enslaved, which is how [[see:Welsh]] later came to mean slave too.
The original Scotland was in Ireland, home of the [[from:Scots]]; the earliest citations of the word refer to part of Ireland.
Tribe from the northern part of Ireland who crossed over to the west of [[see:Scotland]].
Once a Celtic nation, now part of England. The -wall is the same sound as in [[same-root:Wales]], so its people were the Corn Welsh; no corn involved.
Great simply means big, distinguishing it from [[see:Brittany]], the Little Britain across the water.
Celtic nation across the water, a Little Britain beside [[see:Great Britain]].
Roman name for Britain, probably from the Greek name, perhaps from [[from?:Pritani]], the painted people; also a female personification of Britain.
Geoffrey of Monmouth claimed it was named after [[see:Brutus of Troy]], but the hosts think it more likely the Britons named themselves, via [[from:Britannia]].
Trojan who, according to [[see:Geoffrey of Monmouth]], founded New Troy in London and gave his name to [[see:Britain]]; the hosts dismiss the story.

entries.term: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
entries.note: The UK's full official name, a mouthful. It was the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland until Ireland seceded.

entries.term: United States and major outlying territories
entries.note: Unofficial collective name for the US that Jess compares with the long [[see:United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland]].
Spanish for depths, first used on [[see:Christopher Columbus]]'s 1502 voyage. Chroniclers like [[see:Bartolomé de las Casas]] say he thanked God for escaping these depths.
A Spaniard once complicit in the conquest who became a monk and spent 50 years fighting the [[see:encomienda]] and the mistreatment of local peoples.
Spanish labour system giving colonists the right to demand tribute and forced labour from native inhabitants; [[see:Bartolomé de las Casas]] opposed it.
Named by [[see:Flóki Vilgerðarson]] after he saw glaciers, replacing [[see:Snæland]]. One theory says he chose it to deter settlers, unlike [[see:Greenland]].
Viking who tried unsuccessfully to settle there and named [[see:Iceland]] after seeing its ice.
What the island was called before [[see:Flóki Vilgerðarson]] named it [[see:Iceland]].
Named by [[see:Erik the Red]] to attract settlers, according to the Saga of Erik the Red and the Book of Icelanders, though it is less habitable than Iceland.
Exiled from Iceland for murder, he settled and named [[see:Greenland]] in the 10th century.
Official Greenlandic name for [[see:Greenland]], after the Kalaallit, the main Inuit group living there.
Not named after [[unrelated:Iceland]], though Old English spelled Iceland like island. It is unrelated to [[unrelated:isle]] but took its S from it.
Renaissance scholars put its S back to make it look like Latin [[see:insula]]; it then passed the S to the unrelated [[unrelated:island]].
Named for its position on the eastern frontier of the German-speaking lands; its German name is [[see:Österreich]].
German name for [[see:Austria]], meaning eastern empire, because it lay on the eastern frontier of the German-speaking lands.
The north way, because you would follow its coast to go north.
Simply the Spanish for equator; the French call the country [[see:Équateur]].
French name for [[see:Ecuador]], the same as the French word for the equator.
A name used outside a country to refer to it, as opposed to an [[see:endonym]]; exonyms can reveal past power dynamics.
A name a country uses for itself; some, like [[see:Canada]] and [[see:Madagascar]], started as exonyms or misapplied names.
From St. Lawrence Iroquoian [[from:kanata]], village, recorded by [[see:Jacques Cartier]] in 1535–1536. The word for one village came to name the whole country.
Explorer whose accounts of his 1535–1536 voyage record two local men talking about their village, the source of [[see:Canada]].
Named by mistake by [[see:Marco Polo]], who misread an Arabic text about [[from:Mogadishu]]. The islanders had no name for the whole island and adopted his.
The place an Arabic text described, which [[see:Marco Polo]] took to be the island he named [[see:Madagascar]].
Misread an Arabic text about [[see:Mogadishu]] and so coined the name [[see:Madagascar]].
The Albanian name for Albania, one of several surprising endonyms.
The Armenian name for Armenia.
The Hungarian name for Hungary, after the [[see:Magyars]].
A people whose name appears in [[see:Magyarország]], the Hungarian name for Hungary.
The Chinese name for China, meaning middle kingdom.
Mandarin name for America, chosen because mei sounds a bit like America, with [[see:guó]] added.
Mandarin name for England, meaning brave land, chosen because ying sounds a little like England.
Mandarin name for France: a sound similar to France plus [[see:guó]].
Means kingdom or empire. Mandarin adds it to a similar-sounding syllable to name foreign countries, as in [[see:Meiguo]] and [[see:Faguo]].
Little Venice: [[see:Amerigo Vespucci]] thought the stilt houses on Lake Maracaibo looked like [[from:Venice]], giving Veneziola and then Venezuela.
Venezuelan after whom [[see:Bolivia]] is named; Venezuela's official name, [[see:República Bolivariana de Venezuela]], also refers to him.
Named after [[from:Simón Bolívar]], although he was Venezuelan.
Venezuela's official name since 1999, which refers to [[see:Simón Bolívar]].
Like [[same-root:Suriname]] and [[same-root:French Guiana]], probably from a local word meaning land of many waters, for its dense network of rivers and wetlands.
Grouped with [[same-root:Guyana]] and [[same-root:French Guiana]] as probably from a local word meaning land of many waters.
Like [[same-root:Guyana]] and [[same-root:Suriname]], probably from a local word meaning land of many waters.
Named for shallow waters, the opposite of [[see:Honduras]], named for deep ones.
From the Latin, not Spanish, word for silver, [[from:argentum]], by way of the [[from:Río de la Plata]], the river of silver.
An English word that also comes from Latin [[from:argentum]], like [[same-root:Argentina]].
Named from indigenous reports that peoples upriver had silver, and perhaps because it looked silvery; it [[gave:Argentina]] its name.
Named after [[from:Christopher Columbus]]; proposed in the late 18th century by [[see:Francisco de Miranda]] for a unified, independent state of Spanish colonies.
Venezuelan revolutionary who proposed the name [[see:Colombia]] for his planned unified Pan-American state.
Late-18th-century poetic name for the US, from [[from:Christopher Columbus]]. It appears in Washington DC's full name and was a female personification before [[see:Uncle Sam]].
Female personification of France, compared with [[see:Britannia]] and [[see:Columbia]].
Patriotic song about [[see:Columbia]] that was an unofficial national anthem before the Star-Spangled Banner.
Wartime personification of the US that took over from [[see:Columbia]].
From the Portuguese word for [[from:brazilwood]], so named after the tree rather than the [[see:Brazil nut]].
Sometimes said to have given [[see:Brazil]] its name; the hosts say the country is named after [[see:brazilwood]] instead.
Tree native to the Atlantic coastal forests, prized for its red-tinted heartwood, which [[gave:Brazil]] its name.
From Latin [[from:Germania]]; a country with many different names, including [[see:Deutschland]], [[see:Niemcy]] and [[see:Allemagne]].
German name for Germany, from the same word as [[same-root:Dutch]].
Like [[same-root:Deutsch]], it means Germanic people. English applied it to the Low Countries, while the Germans took it for themselves.
A variety of German spoken in America, where [[see:Dutch]] keeps its older sense of Germanic.
Means Germanic people, the same word as [[same-root:Dutch]]; the Germans adopted it for themselves when their states united.
A neighbouring name for Germany that roughly means silent people, or people we don't understand.
French name for Germany, from the Latin name for the region.
Roman name, used by [[see:Tacitus]], for the unconquered barbarian regions; it became [[gave:Germany]].
Land of the [[from:Franks]]. It originally meant only the north of modern France, not the south, where [[see:Occitan]] was spoken.
Germanic tribe with a latinised name of debated meaning: free person, fierceness, or perhaps a javelin-like weapon; they [[gave:France]] its name.
Language of southern France, named, like Occitania, after oc, its word for yes (see [[see:langue d'oc]]); unrelated to [[unrelated:occident]].
Jess asks whether it is related to [[unrelated:Occitan]]; Rob says it isn't.
Author of the Inferno and keen linguist who coined [[see:langue d'oïl]], [[see:langue d'oc]] and related terms for languages, based on their word for yes.
[[see:Dante]]'s term for the language of northern France, after oïl, an Old French way of saying yes.
Term for southern French languages like [[see:Occitan]] and Provençal, whose word for yes was oc; still seen on wine bottles.
[[see:Dante]]'s term for languages, Italian among them, that use sì for yes.
From Latin [[from:Hispania]], originally meaning land of the rabbits, or technically of the [[see:hyrax]].
Latin name the Romans supposedly took from a Carthaginian word for land of the rabbits, really of the [[see:hyrax]]; it [[gave:Spain]].
Rabbit-like animal, like a creepy rabbit without long ears, which the Carthaginian source of [[see:Hispania]] technically refers to.
No one knows where the name comes from; it originally referred to only part of the peninsula.
An exonym, perhaps originally a tribal name, first applied to part of modern Greece; in Greek it is [[see:Hellas]].
The Greek name for Greece, which is why English uses [[see:Hellenic]] for things Greek.
English word for things Greek, related to [[same-root:Hellas]].
Originally just the area around Porto, from Roman [[from:Portus Cale]]; the -gal may instead be a Celtic reference, perhaps to a people.
Roman name for the Porto area. Cale may mean beautiful, perhaps from Greek [[from?:kallos]], or mean port again, making a tautology.
One of Jess's favourite words, discussed in an earlier episode.
A Greek version of the Egyptian [[from:Hut-ka-Ptah]], a temple complex in Memphis to the creator god, extended to the region; it also [[gave:gypsy]].
From [[from:Egypt]]. Like many words for gypsy, it points to a supposedly mysterious place, and this false generalisation makes it a slur for Romani people.
Spanish for gypsy and the name of the gypsy dance, named after [[from:Flanders]] because it seemed far away and mysterious.
The ancient Egyptian name for Egypt, meaning land of black earth, which is seen in [[gave:alchemy]].
An Arabic adaptation referring to the research done in [[from:Kemet]], the land of black earth; [[same-root:chemistry]] is related.
Related to [[same-root:alchemy]].
Named after the [[from:Niger]] river, so its name probably means black.
Country named after the river, probably from Latin for black, or from a local word meaning river, which would make River Niger a tautology; it [[gave:Nigeria]].
An Arabic adaptation meaning land of people with black skin.
Also means land of people with black skin, like [[see:Sudan]].
From Spanish Nueva Guinea, a name given in 1545 by a Spanish explorer who sighted the island's north coast, after [[from:Guinea]].
From a Portuguese form of a word thought to be Berber or Tuareg for black, referring to West African people.
From a Portuguese word for shrimp, meaning river of shrimp; an example of African country names telling a European story.
1884 meeting where European powers divided up Africa and drew borders, one reason names like [[see:Cameroon]] reflect European views.
Shona for houses of stone, a restored indigenous name that replaced [[see:Rhodesia]].
Colonial name replaced by [[see:Zimbabwe]].
A restored indigenous name that replaced [[see:Swaziland]] after the colonial era.
Former name, replaced by [[see:Eswatini]].
Official English spelling of Turkey, reflecting how locals say it and chosen partly so the country isn't named the same as the bird, [[see:turkey]].
The bird is named after the country now called [[from:Türkiye]], probably via Turkish traders; the word first meant [[see:guinea fowl]] before passing to the American bird.
The bird originally called [[see:turkey]], before the name was applied to the American bird.
The accepted English name for the Czech Republic.
Sanskrit word for India found in scriptures from 2,000 years ago, preferred by some, particularly members of the Indian government.
Being used for India at the moment; it is also what English speakers called India before they called it India.
Named after the Moldova River, which legend says takes its name from [[from?:Molda]], a dog that drowned chasing an ox while the founder was hunting.
Legendary hunting dog of the country's founder that drowned chasing an ox across the river, supposedly giving [[see:Moldova]] its name.
